target_customer: Enterprises that run many APIs and need to find and protect them against attacks
problem: APIs became the core of modern applications and were exposed to attacks that web application firewalls and gateways did not catch.
business_model: Enterprise SaaS subscription for an API protection platform

founders.name: Roey Eliyahu
founders.background_notes: Named as CEO and co-founder by VentureBeat and SecurityWeek; no background found in sources opened. Michael Nicosia appears as COO in the company site metadata but not as co-founder, so is not listed.

technical_complexity.rationale: Correlating traffic across millions of APIs with machine learning for discovery and attack detection requires big data pipelines and behavioral models.

defensibility.rationale: Cross customer traffic data improves detection, but later entrants and large vendors entered API security.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Sources reviewed show no acquisition of Salt; Akamai instead bought Noname Security in 2024. Salt remained independent through the Series D in 2022.

market_need_then: APIs were becoming the backbone of applications by 2016, and Salt later reported over 100 enterprise deployments; the need grew strongly by 2021 to 2022 when large rounds closed.

branding.domain_note: salt.security, a .security domain; company earlier known as Secful

identity.voice_and_tone: Enterprise security, API security pioneer positioning

rebrands.why: Not stated; a 2018 trademark filing was by Secful, Inc. and ownership later moved to Salt Security, Inc., exact date unknown

brand_strength.rationale: A short, simple name adopted when the company left stealth and became a recognized API security category leader, though the name is generic and no brand pull evidence was found.

pivots.to: API plus AI agent and MCP server security
pivots.why: Company site describes extending protection to AI agents and MCP servers

outcome_analysis: Salt Security rode the shift to API centric applications, emerged from stealth in 2019 with a $10M seed, and raised $70M in 2021 and $140M at a $1.4B valuation in 2022 led by CapitalG with Sequoia. It remains independent and now extends into AI agent security, so a category-creating enterprise security story explains its success.
notes: SecurityWeek says Series A and B together brought in $50M over the past year before May 2021; aggregator Clay lists Series A $20M (June 2020, Tenaya) and Series B $30M (Dec 2020, Sequoia), unverified individually so recorded as one combined round with stage other. Total after Series D about $271M per VentureBeat, seed 10 + 50 + 70 + 140 is 270, consistent. One aggregator reports a $150M Series D in 2024, treated as an error. Competitors: no source dated near 2016 to 2017 was found, so the list is empty; recent competitor pages are not used. No acquisition or layoff news found for Salt.
